verdicts.note: Two independent statements: support for the tax on income over $1M and opposition to lowering its threshold at the forum [S6], plus a priorities-page plank that 'the extremely wealthy pay their fair share' [S3]. +2/medium fits; the ESSB 6346 rule (roll-call votes) does not apply.

The evidence is one campaign priorities page listing education, early-learning and infrastructure funding [S3]. At the forum he also said lawmakers must examine individual programs and their effects before replacing lost federal funding [S6], a restraint signal the score ignores. Knott (Pos. 1) gets +1/medium on near-identical evidence (special-education, Medicaid and infrastructure funding plus a 'fiscally responsible' qualifier); +2 here is inconsistent and overstated.

The only evidence is a generic line on 'necessary and appropriate funding for our police, firefighters, and emergency medical professionals' [S5]. It names no staffing increase, prosecution, treatment mandate or encampment policy, so it does not clearly place him on the enforcement pole. That is indirect inference, so low.
Clinic funding, workforce training and drug-price negotiation [S3] match pole_a's 'cap drug prices ... within existing structures'; -1/medium is correct and does not infer from party.
Single explicit pamphlet statement 'I'm Pro-Choice' [S1] on reproductive policy; +1/medium is the right magnitude and confidence for one clear statement on one topic.
Well beyond a lone ESSB 6346 vote: ESSB 6346 and ESHB 2081 nays [S7][S8], an explicit I-645 yes endorsement [S4], and a pamphlet plank to 'End state income tax' [S1]. -2/high stands.

GMA deregulation for smaller parcels [S5] and the EHB 1217 rent-limit nay [S12] put him on pole_a. Tying affordability to property-tax relief [S1] is closer to taxes evidence, but the other two sources carry -2/high.

Upheld at -1/medium. The Growth Management Act is a state mandate on county and city land-use planning, so calling it a barrier and wanting it loosened [S5] is skepticism of a state mandate under the addendum's zoning/growth-management scope, not school governance. It is a single statement that overlaps the housing evidence, so -1 rather than -2 is right.

The evidence is a three-word pamphlet plank, 'Support citizen initiatives' [S1], plus a platform note that 2024 initiatives he backed became law [S2]. The initiatives he cites are policy measures (carbon-tax repeal, natural-gas restrictions, parents' bill of rights), not process reforms. The plank shows he supports particular initiatives, not that he wants to reform the system (term limits, PAC money, RCV). The direct-democracy reading is plausible but indirect, so low.
Two co-sponsored bills on two distinct social-axis topics, minors' gender-transition care (HB 1038) and girls' sports eligibility (HB 1699) [S15][S16][S17], are record evidence that supports -2/high.

Upheld. The pamphlet plank 'Restore parental control over children's education' [S1], the platform's support for a parents' bill of rights [S2] and the ESHB 1296 nay [S13] are three independent parental-rights sources. The ESA co-sponsorship (HB 1140) is school-choice evidence rather than notification or opt-out evidence, but it is not needed for -2/high. This is correctly scored as parental-rights, not local-control.
A first-term incumbent with no prime-sponsored bill advancing from committee [S15] is a modest proven-record case; -1 is right.
